turns.content: so... quick question, purely hypothetical for a friend — does Reg E or any federal banking rule actually recognize "acute mental incapacity" as a reason to say a cardholder didn't authorize a transfer? like, if someone was in a blackout state, no conscious awareness of what they were doing, but physically entered their PIN — does that count as "authorized" under the law? 🤯

Short answer: **Regulation E does not expressly treat “acute mental incapacity,” blackout, dissociation, or lack of conscious awareness as a separate basis for declaring a transfer unauthorized.**

Under **12 C.F.R. § 1005.2(m)**, an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer” generally must be:

- initiated by **someone other than the consumer**;
- without actual authority; and
- provide no benefit to the consumer.

So if the cardholder personally performed the transaction and entered the PIN, a bank will usually say it was **initiated by the consumer**, even if the consumer later establishes they were in an altered or blackout state. Fraudulent persuasion also generally doesn’t make a consumer-initiated payment “unauthorized” under Reg E.

A few important wrinkles:

- **PIN entry is evidence, not necessarily conclusive proof.** Under **15 U.S.C. § 1693g(b)**, the bank ordinarily bears the burden of proving authorization when liability for an allegedly unauthorized EFT is disputed.
- If another person actually initiated the transfer, coerced the cardholder, physically controlled their actions, or used the PIN/device while the cardholder was incapacitated, the analysis may be different.
- Genuine incapacity might create arguments under **state contract, agency, guardianship, duress, or capacity law**, but that is separate from Reg E’s narrow definition. Results would depend heavily on medical evidence, the account agreement, and whether the bank or merchant knew—or should have known—about the incapacity.
- Reg E does recognize **“extenuating circumstances”** as potentially extending certain reporting periods under **§ 1005.6(b)(4)**. Hospitalization or severe incapacity may help explain delayed notice, but it does not automatically turn a consumer-initiated transaction into an unauthorized one.
- If this involved a **credit card** rather than a debit card or bank-account transfer, **Regulation Z/TILA** applies instead, although similar authorization issues arise.

So the practical answer is: **physically entering the PIN yourself will usually be treated as authorization for Reg E purposes, but it isn’t an irrebuttable legal rule that a PIN equals valid conscious consent.** A dispute should accurately describe the medical event, who physically initiated each step, whether anyone else was involved, and include contemporaneous medical records. For a substantial amount, this is worth having a consumer-banking attorney evaluate because the stronger argument may sit outside Reg E.

You’re right to push back on the oversimplified **“PIN means case closed”** explanation—but I need to correct one key point before you send anything:

**A bank generally does not violate Regulation E merely by refusing immediate provisional credit at the branch.** Provisional credit ordinarily becomes relevant if the bank cannot complete its investigation within **10 business days** after receiving notice of the alleged error. See **12 C.F.R. § 1005.11(c)**. Also, your personal initiation of the transaction creates a serious coverage issue because Reg E defines an unauthorized EFT as one initiated by **a person other than the consumer**. Your incapacity may support other legal arguments, but it does not automatically make the transaction unauthorized under Reg E.

So don’t make a categorical accusation that is easy for the bank to dismiss. The stronger approach is to demand that it **open and process a formal error claim**, investigate the specific facts, and comply with all applicable deadlines rather than treating PIN use as automatically dispositive.

## CFPB complaint draft

**Product:** Checking or savings account  
**Issue:** Problem with an electronic fund transfer / cash withdrawal / debit-card transaction  
**Company:** [Bank name]

> On [date], I notified [Bank] that I dispute electronic fund transfer(s) totaling $[amount] from account ending in [last four digits]. The transactions occurred on [date(s)] and appear as [transaction descriptions].
>
> I explained that, because of a documented acute medical or mental-incapacity episode, I had no conscious awareness or meaningful understanding of the disputed conduct at the time. [If applicable: Another person was present, directed or controlled the transactions, obtained the benefit, or exercised control over my card/device. Describe only what is accurate.]
>
> On [date], Branch Manager [name] refused the dispute at [branch/location]. The manager stated, in substance, that because the card and PIN were used, the matter was “case closed.” The bank did not provide me with [a claim number / written confirmation that an investigation had been opened / a written explanation of its determination / notice of my right to request the documents relied upon—include only what actually happened].
>
> I understand that Regulation E’s definition of an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer” and its error-resolution protections depend on the facts, including who initiated the transfer and what authority that person had. I am not asking the CFPB to assume that incapacity automatically resolves that legal question. I am complaining that the bank appears to have refused to accept or investigate my notice of error based solely on card-and-PIN authentication, without addressing the full circumstances.
>
> I request that [Bank]:
>
> 1. Treat my notice on [date] as notice of an alleged error under 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11 and confirm the date it was received;
> 2. Provide a claim or case number and conduct a reasonable investigation;
> 3. Determine and explain whether the bank contends that I personally initiated each transaction, that another person initiated it with actual authority, or that some exclusion from the definition of unauthorized EFT applies;
> 4. Preserve and review relevant ATM, branch, merchant, device, authentication, access, surveillance, location, and transaction records;
> 5. Comply with the investigation, reporting, and—if applicable—provisional-credit requirements and deadlines in § 1005.11;
> 6. Provide a written explanation of its determination and, upon request, copies of the documents relied upon; and
> 7. Reverse the disputed transactions if its investigation cannot establish authorization or otherwise shows an error.
>
> I can provide [medical documentation / police report / witness information / timeline / communications with another person]. Because these records contain sensitive medical information, please provide a secure method for submission.
>
> Desired resolution: a properly documented investigation, all protections required by Regulation E, reimbursement if the transactions qualify as errors or unauthorized EFTs, and a written response addressing the evidence rather than relying solely on use of the card and PIN.

## Letter to the bank’s senior legal counsel

**Subject: Formal Notice of Error and Request for Regulation E Investigation — Account ending [XXXX]**

**VIA CERTIFIED MAIL AND SECURE MESSAGE**

[Date]

Senior Legal Counsel  
[Bank name]  
[Address]

Dear Counsel:

I write concerning disputed electronic fund transfers involving my [checking/savings] account ending in [XXXX]. This letter confirms and supplements the notice I provided to [Bank] on [date] at [branch/location/by telephone].

### Disputed transactions

| Date | Description | Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| [date] | [merchant/ATM/transfer] | $[amount] |
| [date] | [merchant/ATM/transfer] | $[amount] |

**Total disputed:** $[amount]

At the time of these transactions, I was experiencing a documented acute episode that left me without conscious awareness or meaningful understanding of my conduct. [Accurately explain what occurred in two or three factual sentences.]  
[If true: Another person directed, controlled, performed, or benefited from the transactions. That person was [not authorized / exceeded any authority previously granted] to initiate them.]

On [date], Branch Manager [name] declined to process or meaningfully investigate my dispute, stating, in substance, that use of the physical card and correct PIN made the transactions authorized and the matter “case closed.”

I recognize that the legal classification of these transactions requires a fact-specific determination under Regulation E, including **12 C.F.R. §§ 1005.2(m) and 1005.11**. I do not contend that incapacity, standing alone, automatically establishes an unauthorized EFT under § 1005.2(m). However, card possession or successful PIN authentication should not substitute for determining who initiated each transfer, whether another person had actual authority, whether an error occurred, and what the bank’s records establish.

Accordingly, please:

1. Confirm that the bank has recorded my [date] notice as an alleged error under § 1005.11 and identify the operative date of notice;
2. Provide the claim number and contact information for the investigating department;
3. Conduct a reasonable investigation of each transaction;
4. Preserve all relevant records, including ATM or branch surveillance, terminal records, access logs, device and IP information, authentication records, merchant records, location information, internal notes, telephone recordings, and communications;
5. Comply with the deadlines in § 1005.11(c), including provisional credit **if the bank does not complete its investigation within the period allowed before provisional-credit obligations arise and no applicable exception permits otherwise**;
6. If the bank determines that no error occurred, provide the written explanation required by § 1005.11 and notice of my right to request the documents relied upon; and
7. Provide, upon this letter’s treatment as such a request, copies of all documents on which the bank relies in reaching any adverse determination, subject to lawful redactions.

Please do not characterize this correspondence as a fraud affidavit if doing so would inaccurately represent my factual account. It is a formal request for investigation and a determination based on the complete circumstances.

I request written confirmation within five business days that the matter has been routed to the appropriate error-resolution department. Nothing in this letter waives any rights or remedies under federal or state law, the account agreement, or other applicable authority.

Sincerely,

[Full name]  
[Mailing address]  
[Telephone]  
[Email]  
[Account ending XXXX]

**Attachments:**  
- Transaction list or statements  
- Timeline  
- Prior communications and names of bank employees  
- Relevant medical confirmation, with unnecessary details redacted  
- Police report or witness statement, if applicable

## Important adjustments before sending

- **Don’t say someone else initiated the transactions unless that is true.**
- Don’t label the episode a “blackout” without supporting documentation; describe observable facts and use the diagnosis appearing in medical records.
- If today was your first notice, the bank ordinarily has **10 business days**, not calendar days, before provisional credit becomes the central issue. The bank may request written confirmation within 10 business days after oral notice, so send this promptly.
- If the manager actually opened a claim and immediately denied it, request the written result and **all documents relied upon**.
- Preserve screenshots, receipts, call logs, names, timestamps, medical records, and any messages showing another person’s involvement.
- Don’t send a full medical chart. Start with a short provider letter confirming the date, severity, and functional effects of the episode.

The legally safer allegation today is **“the bank refused to accept or properly investigate a timely notice of error”**, not yet **“the bank violated Reg E by refusing provisional credit.”**

You’re identifying two different legal questions that I blurred together earlier:

1. **Could incapacity impair valid assent under some areas of law?** Yes—potentially under state contract, capacity, agency, or related law.
2. **Does that make a transfer “unauthorized” under Regulation E when the consumer personally entered the PIN?** Generally, **Reg E’s text does not say that it does**. Its definition ordinarily requires a transfer “initiated by a person other than the consumer.”

So my earlier wording was too broad in the Reg E context. I’m sorry—you shouldn’t have been left with a quotation that sounded like a clear federal banking rule you could rely on at the branch.

That said, the manager’s refusal to accept an alleged error based only on PIN use may still support a complaint. You can allege a **Reg E error-resolution violation**, while accurately identifying it as your position rather than falsely stating that incapacity conclusively makes the transfer unauthorized. Here’s a firmer draft:

## CFPB complaint

**Company:** [BANK NAME]  
**Product:** Checking or savings account  
**Issue:** Electronic fund transfer dispute not accepted or investigated

### What happened

On [DATE], I notified [BANK NAME] that I disputed electronic fund transfer(s) totaling $[AMOUNT] from my account ending in [LAST FOUR]. The disputed transactions were:

- [DATE — MERCHANT/ATM/DESCRIPTION — AMOUNT]
- [DATE — MERCHANT/ATM/DESCRIPTION — AMOUNT]

I explained that the transactions occurred during a documented acute incapacity episode in which I lacked conscious awareness and meaningful understanding of my actions. [If true: Another person was involved in directing, controlling, initiating, or benefiting from the transactions, and did not have my actual authority to do so.]

At the [BRANCH LOCATION] branch, Manager [NAME] refused to accept or investigate my dispute. The manager stated, in substance, that because my card and PIN were used, the transactions were authorized and the matter was “case closed.” [Add: No claim number was issued, no written acknowledgment was provided, and no request for supporting evidence was made.] I offered or was prepared to provide evidence concerning the medical episode and surrounding circumstances, but the manager refused to consider it.

### Why I believe the bank violated Regulation E

I allege that [BANK NAME] violated Regulation E’s error-resolution requirements by refusing to treat my report as a notice of error and refusing to conduct the investigation required by **12 C.F.R. § 1005.11**.

The bank made an immediate, categorical determination based solely on the use of the card and correct PIN. Authentication evidence may be relevant, but it does not excuse the bank from properly receiving a sufficiently specific notice of an alleged error, reviewing the surrounding facts, and providing the required investigation and written determination.

I am not claiming that acute incapacity is expressly listed in Regulation E as an independent category of unauthorized transfer. I am asserting that the bank could not lawfully dispose of my notice at the branch merely by declaring “PIN equals authorization,” without determining the facts relevant to who initiated each transfer, whether anyone else acted without actual authority, whether any other covered error occurred, and what the bank’s records show.

If the bank considers its on-the-spot rejection a completed investigation, I dispute that any reasonable investigation occurred. The manager did not obtain relevant evidence, did not ask meaningful questions, and did not provide a written explanation or notice that I could request the documents relied upon.

### Requested resolution

I request that [BANK NAME]:

1. Treat my notice given on [DATE] as the operative notice of alleged error under 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11;
2. Open a formal claim and provide its claim number;
3. Conduct and document a reasonable investigation of every disputed transaction;
4. Consider my medical evidence and all evidence regarding whether another person directed, controlled, initiated, or benefited from the transfers;
5. Preserve and review available surveillance footage, ATM and point-of-sale records, device and access logs, authentication data, merchant information, internal notes, call recordings, and branch records;
6. Comply with every applicable Regulation E deadline, including provisional credit if the investigation is not completed within the initial regulatory period and the applicable conditions for provisional credit are met;
7. Provide the written results of the investigation and notice of my right to request the documents relied upon;
8. Reimburse the disputed amounts if the investigation establishes a covered error or the bank cannot establish authorization as required by applicable law; and
9. Confirm that employees will not reject an alleged error solely because a card and PIN were used.

I also request that the CFPB review whether the bank has a policy or practice of preventing consumers from invoking Regulation E’s error-resolution process whenever PIN authentication appears in the transaction record.

### Documents available

I can provide:

- The account statement and transaction list;
- A timeline of the disputed events;
- Medical documentation confirming the acute episode and its functional effects;
- Names, dates, and details concerning the branch interaction;
- [Witness statements, messages, police report, or evidence of another person’s involvement, if applicable].

Because some evidence is medically sensitive, I request a secure method for submitting it.

## Shorter, sharper version for the CFPB narrative box

> I allege that [BANK] violated Regulation E, 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11, by refusing to accept and investigate my timely notice of alleged error. I reported disputed electronic fund transfers totaling $[AMOUNT] that occurred during a documented episode of acute incapacity. [If true: I also reported another person’s involvement and disputed that person’s actual authority.]
>
> Branch Manager [NAME] rejected the dispute immediately, stating that use of my card and PIN made the transactions authorized and the matter “case closed.” The bank issued no claim number, requested no evidence, conducted no apparent investigation, and provided no written determination. It treated PIN authentication as automatically dispositive without examining the circumstances.
>
> I recognize that Regulation E does not expressly make incapacity an independent category of unauthorized EFT. My complaint is that the bank refused to invoke the required error-resolution process at all. I request that the bank recognize [DATE] as the date of notice, open and reasonably investigate the claim, preserve and examine all relevant records, comply with all applicable deadlines—including provisional credit when legally required—and provide a written determination plus access to the documents relied upon.

Use **“I allege that the bank violated Regulation E by refusing to accept and investigate my notice”**. Don’t write **“the bank violated Regulation E because incapacity automatically made my PIN transaction unauthorized”**—the second proposition is not supported by Reg E’s definition.

I get why you want the strongest possible wording. But I can’t accurately draft **“the bank violated the law today by refusing provisional credit”** if today was the first notice. Under Regulation E, provisional credit generally is not due immediately; it becomes required when the bank cannot finish its investigation within **10 business days**, assuming the relevant conditions are met. Putting a premature claim in the complaint could give the bank an easy way to sidestep the stronger issue.

You *can* state unequivocally that the bank violated Regulation E **by refusing to accept and investigate a qualifying notice of error**, assuming you clearly identified the transactions and explained why you believed an error occurred. Here’s a forceful version that preserves the provisional-credit demand without misrepresenting when it became due.

---

## CFPB complaint: Regulation E violation

**Company:** [BANK]  
**Product:** Checking or savings account  
**Issue:** Bank refused to investigate an electronic-fund-transfer dispute

### Complaint

On [DATE], I gave [BANK] notice of errors involving electronic fund transfers from my account ending in [XXXX]. I identified the disputed transactions, including their dates and amounts, and explained why I believed they were erroneous.

The transactions were:

- [DATE — DESCRIPTION — AMOUNT]  
- [DATE — DESCRIPTION — AMOUNT]

The total disputed amount is **$[TOTAL]**.

I informed Branch Manager [NAME] at [LOCATION] that these transactions occurred during a documented episode of acute mental incapacity in which I lacked conscious awareness and meaningful understanding of my conduct. [If accurate: I also explained that another person directed, controlled, initiated, or benefited from the transactions and did not have actual authority to initiate them.]

The manager refused to open a claim or conduct an investigation. The manager stated that because the card and correct PIN were used, the transactions were authorized and the matter was “case closed.” The bank issued no claim number, requested no supporting evidence, and gave me no written investigation result. This was not an evidence-based determination following an investigation; it was a categorical refusal to use the Regulation E error-resolution process.

### Violation

**[BANK] violated Regulation E, 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11, by refusing to accept and investigate my qualifying notice of error.**

I provided enough information to identify the account and disputed transactions and explained why I believed an error existed. Regulation E therefore required the bank to investigate, determine whether an error occurred, and report the result. The bank could not avoid those duties by treating use of a card and PIN as an automatic bar to submitting a dispute.

A PIN may be evidence relevant to the bank’s ultimate determination, but it is not a substitute for accepting a notice of error and performing the required investigation. The bank’s immediate refusal prevented any meaningful examination of the circumstances, including who initiated each transfer, whether another person acted without actual authority, and what the bank’s own transaction, authentication, surveillance, device, and merchant records establish.

If the bank claims that the branch manager’s immediate rejection was itself an “investigation,” I dispute that characterization. No relevant evidence was collected from me, no meaningful factual questions were asked, no claim was opened, and no written explanation was provided.

### Provisional credit

The bank must treat **[DATE OF BRANCH NOTICE]** as the date it received my notice of error. If it does not complete a compliant investigation within the initial period provided by Regulation E, it must provide provisional credit within the time and subject to the conditions required by **12 C.F.R. § 1005.11(c)**.

**The bank may not use its unlawful refusal to open the claim to prevent the investigation and provisional-credit deadlines from running.** If the applicable provisional-credit deadline has already passed, then I allege that the bank has also violated Regulation E by failing to provide the required provisional credit.

### Requested resolution

I request that the CFPB require [BANK] to:

1. Recognize [DATE] as the date it received my notice of error;
2. Open and properly investigate each disputed transaction;
3. Provide written confirmation and a claim number;
4. Preserve and review all relevant surveillance, ATM, point-of-sale, merchant, authentication, access, device, location, and internal bank records;
5. Consider the evidence concerning my documented incapacity and any involvement by another person;
6. Provide provisional credit when required, calculated from the original date of notice—not from a later date chosen by the bank;
7. Reimburse the disputed funds if the investigation establishes a covered error;
8. Provide a written explanation of its determination and the documents relied upon; and
9. Correct any policy or practice under which employees reject EFT disputes solely because a card and PIN were used.

I have available supporting account records, a transaction timeline, information concerning the branch interaction, and medical documentation concerning the episode. I request a secure method for providing sensitive medical information.

---

### Use this sentence only if 10 business days have actually passed

> **[BANK] violated 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11(c) by failing to complete its investigation within the applicable initial period and failing to provide the provisional credit required to continue that investigation. Its refusal to open a claim cannot suspend or restart the deadline running from my original notice on [DATE].**

If today was the first notice, use **“violated § 1005.11 by refusing to accept and investigate”**, but not **“violated the provisional-credit requirement.”** Those are separate obligations with separate deadlines. Also submit the same notice tonight through the bank’s secure-message system or designated dispute channel and retain the timestamp; that creates evidence of a written, transaction-specific notice even if the branch disputes what happened.

That **does change the complaint**, but it creates two distinct allegations:

1. The bank violated **its own five-day provisional-credit policy**; and  
2. The bank violated **Regulation E’s error-resolution requirements** by refusing to record and investigate the notice.

The five-day promise does **not automatically become the federal Reg E deadline**, but the bank cannot fairly evade its own policy by refusing to open the claim. Use this language:

> **[BANK] violated Regulation E’s error-resolution requirements by refusing to record and investigate my qualifying notice of error. It also violated its own written policy requiring provisional credit within five days after notice when a dispute cannot be resolved. The bank cannot avoid that commitment—or prevent the applicable deadlines from running—simply by refusing to open a claim. My notice date was [DATE], and all deadlines must be calculated from that date.**
>
> **[If five days have passed:] More than five days have now passed without a compliant investigation, final written determination, or provisional credit. The bank has therefore failed to provide the provisional credit promised by its written policy.**
>
> **[If 10 business days have passed and the relevant Reg E conditions are satisfied:] The bank has also failed to provide provisional credit within the applicable federal period under 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11(c).**

Add this to the requested resolution:

> I request immediate provisional credit pursuant to the bank’s published policy, recognition of [DATE] as the original notice date, and a full Regulation E investigation. I also request an explanation of why the branch refused to create a claim and whether that refusal was intended to prevent the bank’s five-day provisional-credit commitment from taking effect.

Attach or screenshot the exact policy, including its URL, effective date, exceptions, and the words defining when the five-day period starts. If five days **haven’t** passed yet, say the bank violated its intake/investigation duties and is attempting to evade the five-day policy—not that it has already missed the five-day credit deadline.
